She captured 26 cockroaches from the same area 17 of which were not marked. Estimate the population in the area. INTERACTIONS BETWEEN POPULATION Individual organisms in the population do not live in isolation in a community. They are continuously interacting with each other in the following ways:  Competition  Predation  Mutualism  Parasitism COMPETITION As the population of the individuals increase, the resources become limited and the organisms compete for them. Examples of resources competed for include, food, space, mates, etc. Competition is of two types; 1. Interspecific competition ; this is the competition between organisms of different species, e.g. the competition between goats and cattle for pastures. 2. Intraspecific competition; this is the competition between organisms of the same species, e.g. the competition between goats for grass. PREDATION This is the relationship between a predator and the prey. A predator is an organism that hunts and kills another organism (prey) for food. A prey is an organism that is hunted and killed for food.

1810dcba39a5b88b2552a265834517ea08e79e32.document: The graph showing the predator-prey relationship Description and explanation of the graph: The population of the prey is higher than that of the predator at the start. This leads to an increase in the number of predators. The prey reaches a peak earlier than the predators. Further increase in the predator population leads to a decrease in the prey population due to the fact that they are being fed on by the predators. When the number of prey goes down, the predators starve and this makes their population to go down. When the predator number decreases below that of the prey, the population of the prey increases again due to the fact that the predator s are few which would feed on them. Note. Both the predator and prey control the population of each other. Adaptations of predators that enable them to feed on prey 1. They have keen eyesight to see their prey. 2. They have strong jaw muscles to tear flesh of the prey. 3. They have sharp claws to hold and kill their prey. 4. They move very fast to enable them chase the prey. 5. They have streamlined bodies to cut through air during movement. 6. Some have very sharp canines to tear flesh of their prey. 7. They have colours, which help them to camouflage. Adaptations of the prey to avoid being eaten by predators 1. They perceive sound with high accuracy and are able to sense their predators at a distance. 2. They are very fast in movement to escape from their predators. 3. They have developed structures for defense such as horns. 4. They normally move in groups to scare their predators. 5. They prefer to stay in areas, which give them good visibility such as grasslands.

5bdee2c09004572ab4827b57fddbbd0719aefec7.document: 6. They have colours, which help them to camouflage. 7. Mimicry; this is where a palatable harmless organism attains colours of an unpalatable harmful organism and it is confused for a harmful organism. FEEDING RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN ORGANISMS SYMBIOSIS This is the relationship between two organisms of different species in which both organisms derive benefits from the association. Examples 1. In the stomach of cattle and sheep there are bacteria. These bacteria help to digest cellulose, which is used by the cow. The bacteria benefits by getting food and shelter from the cow. 2. The nitrogen -fixing bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants. The bacteria provide nitrates to the plant by converting nitrogen to nitrates and the bacteria are protected in the root nodules. The bacteria may also use sugars produced by the plant during photosynthesis 3. The lichen is composed of a fungus and filament of algae. The fungus provides water and mineral salts to the algae and the fungus benefits by using the sugars produced by the algae COMMENSALISM This is the relationship between the organisms of different species in which only one organism (commensal) benefits but the other organism neither benefits nor loses. Examples. 1. The shark and the ramora. The ramora is a small fish that lives as a commensal attached to the shark by its sucker. When the shark feeds, the ramora feeds on left overs of the shark. The shark neither benefits nor loses. 2. The cattle/buffalos and the egret. The egret gets food in form of insects forced to fly by grazing animals. The cattle do not gain and do not lose. PARASITISM This is the association between two organisms in which one (the parasite) is nutritionally dependent on the other (host). The host is harmed in the process. Parasites are divided into two categories: 1. Endo-parasites; these are parasites that live inside th e body of the host, e.g. plasmodium and HIV 2. Ectoparasites; these are parasites which live outside the body of the host, e.g. ticks, lice and flea.

a78fd2fd2c433af0109001f0c69af88fb12dae5b.document: Parasites can also be described as: Obligate parasites; these are parasites which cannot live without their hosts. Examples of obligate parasites are plasmodium and HIV. Facultative parasites; these are parasites that can spend some time outside the bodies of their hosts. E.g. Ticks. Incidental parasites; these are organisms that are not usually parasite but may become parasitic due to factors like lack of their normal food, increase in their numbers, etc. an example is Entamoeba gingivalis. Problems faced by parasites i) Finding the host may be difficult since most hosts keep on moving from one place to another. ii) Deficiency of food in case the host has similar deficiency. iii) They may be killed by the hosts’ immune reactions. iv) Death of parasites incase the host dies due to starvation. v) Inabilities to live in a wide range of environment since most of them have low power of locomotion i.e. they are not able to live freely. To overcome some of these problems, the parasites have a number of adaptations so as to cope up with their mode of life. General adaptations of parasites 1. They have means of attachment to the host. 2. They have penetrative devices for entering and feeding on the host 3. They show degeneration of unnecessary organs and systems to reduce on their body size in order to fit in the host. e.g. eyes 4. They produce many eggs, seeds or spores to enhance their survival. 5. They have vector intermediate hosts 6. They produce resistant stages to survive in periods when they are outside the host Types of hosts 1. Intermediate host: This is the host in which the larvae stage of parasites develops from (secondary host). 2. Primary host (infinite host): This is the host in which sexual reproduction of a parasite occurs from.

37a80806b0761ac68e3d2d057d5f860011f63a66.document: EXAMPLES OF PARASITES 1. PLASMODIUM SPP This is a protozoan parasite that causes malaria. It is transmitted from one person to another by the female anopheles mosqui to. The mosquito acts as the vector. Life cycle of plasmodium  Mosquitoes bite a human and inject saliva to stop blood from clotting in its alimentally canal.  In the process hundreds of parasites are moved from the mosquito into the person.  The parasites move to the liver through the circulatory system.  They burrow in the liver cells and reproduce very fast.  Within one to two weeks, the daughter cells break out of the liver and move to invade the red blood cells.  In the red blood cells the y reproduce rapidly causing the cells to rapture and invade other red blood cells.  They then attack new red blood cells causing them to rapture also.  If a mosquito sucks blood from an infected person, it will take up these parasites in the red blood cells.  The parasites reproduce in the mosquito and migrate to the salivary glands ready to infect the next person when that mosquito bites. Note. Each time the daughter cells of plasmodia are released, thousands of red blood cells rapture and the patient exper iences chills accompanied by shivering and sweating. The patient may also become anemic due to loss of red blood cells. Control of malaria  Spraying the walls of dwelling places with insecticides. The insecticide may also be sprayed directly on the mosquito vector.  Draining all stagnant water to prevent mosquitoes from breeding there.  Removing broken bottles, old tins, old car tyres, e.t.c in which water collects. This also prevents breeding of mosquitoes.  Sleeping under mosquito nets  Treating the infected people using anti-malarial drugs.

70705bef50297f124087d02fe78dd70b5a43ee0f.document: 2. THE TAPEWORM These are flatworms belonging to phylum platyhelminthes. There are two common species known. i) Taenia sagnata (beef tape worm) ii) Taenia solium (pork tape worm) They live in the small intestine of humans attached to the wall of the small intestine by hooks and suckers. They absorb nutrients from the digested food. Life cycle of a tapeworm  Within the infected human being, the segments containing fertilized eggs break off and pass out in feaces.  These eggs then tend to become attached to leaf blades of vegetation.  When the eggs are eaten by the pig or cow depending on the species of the tapeworm, they develop into embryos.  The released embryos burrow through the intestinal walls into the blood, which transports them to the muscles.  Within the muscles they develop into bladder worms.  If uncooked or partially cocked, meat from an infected cow or pig is eaten, the bladder worms are released in the intestines where they develop into tapeworms. Control 1. Avoid eating raw or half cooked meat. 2. By regular de-worming of infected individuals 3. By proper disposal of wastes 4. Inspection of meat before it is considered fit for human consumption. Adaptations of tapeworms to parasitic life i) They have lost the alimentally canal hence absorb already digested food over the entire body surface by diffusion. ii) They have a thick cuticle to prevent attack by digestive enzymes of the host. iii) They produce substances that inactivate the enzymes of the host. iv) Each mature proglotids of the tapeworm c ontains both male and female reproductive organs (hermaphrodites) hence fertilizes itself. v) They produce large numbers of eggs to ensure their survival. vi) They have suckers for attachment to intestinal walls. This prevents the tape worm from being dislodged by host peristaltic movements vii) They have resistant stages in their lifecycles with secondary and intermediate hosts to ensure survival during adverse conditions. viii) There is loss of unwanted organs like locomotally organs, eyes, etc. to ensure that they occupy as little space as possible within the host.

SCHISTOSOMES These are flat worms known as flukes. They are parasites that cause bilharzia (schistosomiasis) Life cycle  Schistosoma requires the use of two hosts to complete its life cycle  Eggs are shed in faeces or urine of an infected human  Eggs can survive up to a week in dry land  If feaces end up in water, larvae called miracidia hatch  Find a snail and penetrate its foot  Transform into primary sporocysts ( another larval form)  Primary sporocysts multiply asexually into secondary sporocysts  Travel to snails hepatopancreas  Multiply asexually into many cercariae ( another larval form)  Cercariae exit the snail into the water (survive for about 48 hours )  Swim and attach to human skin with suckers  Find a suitable spot (e.g a hair follicle) and penetrate the skin using special enzymes  Transform into schistosomulae as they enter(another larval form)  Only head parts enter, tails remain behind  After a few days in rain, enter into the blood stream through dermal lymphatic vessels or blood venules  Travel in blood stream to get to specific blood veins  Schistosoma reaches maturity in 6-8 weeks in humans  Developed adult male and female find each other and pair up  Males make a gynaecophoric channel for longer thinner females to reside  The pair travel to rectal and mesenteric veins  Attach to venous wall with ventral and oral suckers  Females lay eggs on endothelial linning of the venous capillary walls  Some eggs are flushed by circulating blood ending up causing inflammation in organs like liver, lungs  Most eggs travel to lumen of intestinal tract( for S. mansoni) ureters and bladder(for S. haematobium)  Mature eggs produce special enzymes and can penetrate many membranes like renal veins or intestinal walls  Eggs get out of the body in faeces or urine  Cycle starts again

This is a gradual change in the composition of organisms in the area. There are two types of succession. 1. Primary succession 2. Secondary succession 1. Primary succession This is a type of succession where life begins from a bare rock or new pond, which has neve r been occupied by living organisms before. The pioneer plants in such areas are those, which can with stand dry conditions with low water content and high temperatures. The first organisms to inhabit such an area are called pioneer organisms. Stages of succession on a bare rock Stage 1 The lichens grow on bare rock. When they die, they decompose to form a thin layer of soil, which traps some moisture. Stage 2 Mosses start growing on the soil formed by the decayed lichens. When the mosses die, they decay to form more soil. Stage 3 The soil formed favours the growth of ferns.

During this stage some rodents may start coming in. Stage 5 Shrubs are formed and they finally develop into trees. The trees form the climax community after which no other changes take place. Succession in a new water pond It takes several years for a climax community to be established. Any disturbance at any one level causes the process of succession to go back to the initial stages and it later on re -establishes. The ability of the community to re establish after a disturbance is known as resilience. A climax community is the final steady community that develops at the end of the succession process. Characteristics of primary succession  A pioneer community has very few species of plants and animals.  The pioneer vegetation is shallow rooted  The pioneer community colonizes a bare rock.  It takes a long time to reach the climax community. 2. Secondary succession This is a type of succession, which takes place in an area, which has ever been occupied by organisms and des troyed by disasters like fire, floods and human activities. This type of succession is faster than primary succession. Characteristics of secondary succession  It begins on already formed soil or land.  The pioneer community has a variety of plant and animal species.  It takes a short time to reach the climax community  The pioneer vegetation is of higher plants which are deep rooted. Introduction The civil engineering industry is one of the largest and most economically significant industries in the modern world. It encompasses the planning, design, construction, and maintenance of infrastructure such as roads, bridges, dams, buildings, and water s ystems. However, it is also an industry characterised by extensive use of manual and semi-skilled labour, and wherever large numbers of people are employed in physically demanding work, the question of safety becomes paramount. In Tanzania, as in many developing countries, construction site safety has historically been treated as a secondary concern, often neglected in the rush to complete projects within budget and schedule constraints. This attitude must change. For proper nati onal development and economic growth — supported by rapid industrialisation — a stable, productive, and healthy workforce is essential. Management responsibilities: It is the duty of every construction firm's management to strive to meet workers' social, psychological, and welfare needs. This includes taking concrete steps to humanise the work environment — making it safer, more dignified, and more conducive to long-term productivity. 2. Key Definitions Before examining the causes, consequences, and preventive measures for construction site accidents, it is essential to establish clear definitions of the core concepts. 2.1 Safety Safety is a multidimensional concept that is often difficult to define precisely because it depends on the inter relationship of several technical, human, and environmental factors. In common usage, safety is expressed inversely with accident rate: High accident rate = Low safety; Low accident rate = High safety More formally, safety can be defined as: • The state of being safe — freedom from danger, risk, or injury. • The condition of enterprise operations in which, by controlling hazards, accident-free production is achieved. 2.2 Risk Risk involves two dimensions: • The probability (likelihood) that a particular event will occur. • The potential magnitude of loss or harm that would result if the event does occur. Definition: Risk is the probability that some event will cause an undesirable outcome, combined with the assessment of the potential amount of loss. Example: Working at heights without fall protection presents a high risk because both the probability of falling and the severity of injury are significant.

639bbc9a686cc731740be43b2aade0e200115b0e.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page 2.3 Hazard A hazard is an unsafe condition or activity that, if left uncontrolled, can contribute to or directly cause an accident. Unlike risk, a hazard is an objective condition or act, it is the source of potential harm. Common examples of hazards on construction sites: • Untidy, cluttered working areas (trip and fall hazards) • Missing or damaged machine guards • Broken or defective ladders and scaffolding • Slippery surfaces due to water, mud, or oil • Exposed electrical wiring • Unguarded excavations and open trenches 2.4 Accident An accident is an unexpected and undesirable event that results in damage to property or harm to persons. The key characteristic is that it is unforeseen , neither planned nor anticipated. Two complementary definitions are widely accepted: • An event which is unexpected, or the cause of which is unforeseen. • Any occurrence that interrupts normal work activities and whose cause was unforeseen. Conditions that may predispose workers to accidents include: • Lack of proper safety equipment at work sites • Long working hours leading to fatigue and reduced alertness • Improper living conditions affecting health and concentration • Improper or unsafe working conditions

e762de29e29ff8f0b232e138996d5e2b07c81b0d.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page 3. Why Does Safety Matter? The frequent occurrence of accidents on construction sites leads to multiple forms of loss, which affect not only the workers and their families, but also the contractor, client, and the industry at large. Type of Loss Explanation Loss of Labour Skilled workers incapacitated or killed represent a major human and economic cost. Loss of Money Compensation claims, medical costs, legal fees, and equipment repair all add up. Loss of Time Work stoppages for investigation, rehabilitation, and re-staffing delay projects. Loss of Materials Damaged equipment, tools, and materials must be replaced at additional cost. Reputational Loss: Beyond direct costs, frequent accidents result in a severe loss of reputation for the contractor or builder, making it harder to win future tenders and maintain client trust. 4. Construction Safety Statistics in Tanzania Construction is consistently ranked among the most hazardous industries worldwide, and Tanzania is no exception. Key Findings (CRB/OSHA Study): A study commissioned by the Contractors' Registration Board (CRB) and conducted by the Occupational Safety & Health Authority (OSHA) recorded 150 accidents on 63 sites over a single 12-month period. Broader Impact (TACECA): According to the Tanzania Civil Engineering & Contractors' Association (TACECA), many hundreds of thousands of workers across the country suffer serious injuries annually in the construction industry. 4.1 Breakdown of Fatalities by Accident Type An analysis of construction fatalities reveals the following distribution: Cause of Fatality Percentage (%) Falls from height 56% Trapped by collapsing/overturning objects 21% Struck by moving vehicle 10% Contact with electricity 5% Struck by falling object 4% Contact with moving machinery 3% Exposure to harmful substances 1%

Causes of Construction Site Accidents Construction accidents generally arise from three broad categories of causes: • Human causes • Faulty working methods (related to objects and equipment) • Structural failures 5.1 Human Causes Human behaviour and attitude are at the root of many construction site accidents. These include: • Lack of knowledge — workers unaware of hazards or safe procedures • Lack of skill — insufficient training for the tasks being performed • Lack of interest in work — demotivated workers who are careless • Carelessness in supervision — supervisors failing to enforce safety standards • Other personal factors — illness, fatigue, substance use, personal problems affecting concentration 5.2 Faulty Working Methods (Related to Objects) Many accidents arise not from personal failings but from systemic problems in how work is organised and carried out: • No use of protective equipment — workers exposed to hazards without PPE • No site layout planning — poorly organised sites increase collision and confusion risks • Improper storage of materials — unstable stacks, blocked access routes, misplaced heavy items 5.3 Structural Failures Structural failures can result in catastrophic outcomes, including mass casualties. Common causes include: • Failure of foundation — inadequate ground investigation or bearing capacity • Faulty design — errors in structural calculations, detailing, or specification • Natural calamities — earthquakes, floods, severe winds that exceed design parameters

06d90fdce5f7e6540f3585273a560f5191fbe392.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page 6. Specific Factors Causing Accidents on Construction Sites Beyond the broad categories, several specific operational factors contribute to construction accidents. These include: • Improper scaffolding procedures • Defective equipment • Wall and roof collapses • Inadequate supervision • Dropped loads • Lack of information through warnings • Inappropriate use of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) • Untidy site conditions 6.1 Improper Scaffolding Procedures Scaffolding-related accidents are among the most common and serious on construction sites. There are four principal failure modes: 6.1.1 Falls from Scaffolding Falls occur due to the absence of critical fall protection measures: • Absence of a guardrail system along scaffold platforms • No personal fall arrest systems (harnesses, lanyards, anchor points) • Improper access — ladders incorrectly positioned, angled, or secured 6.1.2 Electrocution Electrical hazards arise when scaffolding comes into contact with live power lines: • Workers accidentally touching energised overhead power lines • Working materials, scaffold frames, or planks contacting energised lines 6.1.3 Impacts from Objects Falling from Scaffolds Workers at lower levels are at risk from: • Tools and materials dropped or knocked off the scaffold platform • Scaffold components dropped during erection or dismantling operations 6.1.4 Collapse of the Scaffold Scaffold collapse can injure many workers simultaneously: • Tall, unstable scaffold structures not properly secured with ties, guys, and braces • Overloading the scaffold beyond its rated capacity • Erecting scaffolds on soft or uneven ground without proper base plates

5a6c02686be733232187f092b8d1aee07b579408.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page Most Important Safety Factors for Scaffolding • Train all workers before they are permitted on or near scaffolding • Begin erection on a firm, solid, and level supporting foundation • Install and connect all components correctly per manufacturer specifications • Do not overload platforms with construction materials • Ensure the platform is fully planked — no gaps • Use guardrail systems and personal fall arrest systems at all times • Inspect the scaffold before starting each working shift • Provide a safe means of access and egress (properly secured ladders) 6.2 Defective Equipment Equipment defects and mechanical failures are a significant source of construction injuries. Two pieces of equipment are particularly prominent: Forklifts: Forklifts are used on practically all construction sites for material handling. Due to their size, complexity, and load capacity, defects in forklift design or manufacture — such as brake failure, steering failure, or hydraulic faults — can result in severe injuries including broken bones, crush injuries, and spinal damage. Cranes: Crane accidents are some of the most common and catastrophic on construction sites. Even experienced crane operators cannot prevent accidents if the machine has defective or missing components — leading to structural collapse, dropped loads, head injuries, spinal damage, and fractures. 6.3 Wall and Roof Collapses The sudden collapse of walls or roofs can trap and kill workers with little warning. Primary causes include: • Lack of proper wall or ceiling support — particularly in buildings under construction or during partial demolition • Old or inadequate building materials — older buildings being demolished may collapse unexpectedly • Excessive moisture — snow accumulation on a roof, or rainwater undermining a building foundation 6.4 Lack of Information Through Warnings Workers who are not adequately warned of hazards are at greatly increased risk. Effective warning systems use standardised signs, colour codes, and tags. 6.4.1 Warning Signs — Colour Coding System Sign Type Colour Meaning NOTICE Blue on white Informs personnel of general information or content SAFETY Green on white Gives instructions and suggestions regarding safe practice CAUTION Black on yellow Signals potentially hazardous situations that could cause minor to moderate injury

a39acf4b6c300734039b5e38472f63e21d79faba.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page WARNING Black on orange Indicates a hazard that could cause moderate to severe injury or death DANGER Red on black/white Marks an immediate hazard that could cause death or serious injury BIOHAZARD White or black on red Signals the presence of potentially infectious biological hazards 6.4.2 Warning Tags and Barricade Tape Warning tags mark temporary hazards on specific equipment or locations. They include a signal word and a major message that can be recognised by colour. Common tags include: • "OUT OF ORDER" (yellow triangle) — equipment or area not in service • "DANGER — DO NOT START" (red on black/white) — equipment must not be operated • "WARNING" (black on orange) — hazardous condition present Barricade tape is used to identify temporary hazardous locations. Different colour combinations denote specific hazard types: • Red/white diagonal stripes — Fire prevention and protection equipment • Black/white diagonal stripes — Housekeeping and aisle marking • Magenta/yellow — Radiation hazards • Green/white — Safety and first aid equipment • Blue/white — Defective machinery • Orange/white — Traffic and caution warning • Yellow/black — Physical hazards

16e7f28dd13fd8b96565dd7849acd017645f2a7b.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page 6.5 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) refers to any device or clothing designed to protect the wearer from specific hazards. It is important to understand that PPE does nothing to eliminate the hazard at its source; it is the last line of defence that reduces the severity of injury should a hazard be encountered. PPE is broadly categorised as follows: PPE Category Examples and Application Head Protection Hard hats / safety helmets — protect against falling objects and head impacts Hearing Protection Earplugs or earmuffs — required in high-noise environments (>85 dB) Respiratory Protection Dust masks, respirators — for areas with dust, fumes, or toxic gases Eye and Face Protection Safety glasses, goggles, face shields — protect against flying particles, splashes, UV radiation Hand Protection Gloves (leather, cut-resistant, chemical-resistant) — depending on task Foot Protection Safety boots with steel toe-caps and puncture-resistant soles Protective Clothing High-visibility vests, overalls, chemical-resistant suits Critical Note: PPE is a barrier protection measure only. The hierarchy of hazard control places engineering controls and elimination above PPE. PPE should always be complemented by other preventive measures. 6.6 Untidy Site Conditions A poorly maintained construction site is a major source of accidents, particularly slips, trips, and falls. Good housekeeping is a fundamental safety requirement and must be enforced throughout the working day, not just at the end of shifts. Good housekeeping practices include: • Cleaning up broken glass and sharp debris immediately • Picking up loose objects from walkways and working areas • Emptying, decontaminating, and cleaning containers used for hazardous substances • Cleaning equipment and work surfaces after use • Disinfecting areas that have come into contact with potentially infectious materials • Keeping walkways and floors free of cords, debris, boxes, or other trip hazards • Keeping the overall work area neat and organised • Cleaning up spills immediately — liquid on hard surfaces creates serious slip hazards

6ddc607daf853a7fe64d32d46c9400107bad0fd7.document: CEB 8412 – Industrial Building Construction | Lecture 7: Safety at Construction Site Mbeya University of Science and Technology (MUST) Page 7. Construction Site Safety Tips The following practical tips form the foundation of a safe construction site culture. Every worker and manager must understand and practice these measures. 1. Wear PPE on site at all times — PPE is your last line of defence when you come into contact with a hazard. Always wear a hard hat and safety boots at minimum; add task-specific PPE as required (gloves, goggles, harness, etc.). 2. Do not start work without a site induction — Each site has its own unique hazards and work operations. The induction brief is not optional; it is your introduction to site -specific risks and emergency procedures. 3. Keep a tidy site — Construction work is inherently messy, but workers must maintain their work areas throughout their shift. Pay particular attention to high -risk areas such as access routes and emergency escape routes. 4. Never work in unsafe areas — Do not work at height without suitable guardrails or other fall prevention. Do not enter unsupported trenches. Ensure safe access to your work location at all times. Never work below crane loads or other overhead operations. 5. Report defects and near misses — If you notice a problem — a broken tool, an exposed wire, an unstable scaffold — report it immediately to your supervisor. Near misses must also be reported: they are warnings of future accidents. Action cannot be taken if management is not aware of the issue.

Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) 8.1 Definition and Purpose A Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) is a systematic process used to identify, assess, and eliminate or mitigate potential hazards associated with specific job tasks before work commences. It is a proactive tool — identifying hazards before accidents occur, rather than investigating after. The JHA process involves: • Breaking down the job into individual sequential tasks • Identifying potential hazards associated with each task • Conducting a risk assessment to determine the likelihood and severity of each hazard • Developing preventive measures aimed at eliminating or controlling each hazard 8.2 Focus of the JHA A JHA focuses on the relationship between four key elements: • The worker — skills, experience, physical condition • The task — what is being done and how • The tools — equipment and materials involved • The work environment — site conditions, weather, surrounding activities Ideally, once uncontrolled hazards are identified, steps are taken to eliminate them entirely. Where elimination is not possible, they should be reduced to an acceptable risk level through engineering controls, administrative controls, or PPE. 8.3 Who Develops a JHA? A JHA should be developed by anyone knowledgeable about the job, including: • Managers and project directors • Supervisors and foremen • Team leaders • Experienced employees who carry out the task Involving workers in the JHA process is best practice — they have first-hand knowledge of the practical hazards involved in their tasks. 8.4 Steps in Conducting a JHA 6. Break down the job into its basic sequential steps 7. Identify the potential hazards associated with each step 8. Inspect materials for sharp edges prior to handling. Gloves are required when handling tools and materials. Eye Injury Utilise safety glasses with side-shields at all times during excavation. Underground Service Strike Contact the underground utility authority 48 hours prior to beginning work to mark all underground utility locations. Trench Collapse Trench depth shall be kept at 36 inches (approx. 900 mm) or less. A Competent Person in excavation shall evaluate the weather, soil, and work progress to determine if collapse risk is present. Equipment Failure The excavator shall be inspected daily using an approved checklist. This inspection will be performed by trained operators; a record will be kept onsite. Struck by Equipment All workers shall wear high-visibility vests at all times. Trained operators shall maintain visibility of the work area and swing radius. A designated path for the excavator shall be established. Equipment Tip-over The excavator shall not operate on unlevel terrain where tip-over is possible. The operator's manual shall be consulted regarding terrain restrictions. Fuel Spill Fuel shall be kept in approved containers. Fuel containers shall be properly labelled. Refuelling shall be carried out away from ignition sources. Trip Hazards At the end of each working day, delineators and danger tape shall identify open trench areas. Trenches shall be backfilled as soon as possible.

Steps to Follow After a Construction Site Accident Despite all preventive measures, accidents may still occur. When they do, it is essential that a structured and legally compliant response is immediately undertaken. The following four steps must be followed in order. Step 1: Obtain Medical Care The immediate priority after any injury is the health and safety of the injured person. Even if the injury appears minor, a medical professional must diagnose and treat the injury before the person is permitted to return to work. Delayed treatment can worsen injuries that initially seem superficial. • Call for emergency medical assistance immediately if the injury is serious • Administer first aid while waiting for professional help if trained to do so • Do not move an injured worker if a spinal or neck injury is suspected • Ensure the injured worker does not return to work without medical clearance Step 2: Record the Details of the Accident If the injured worker is physically capable, they should immediately record the key facts of the accident, including: • Time and date of the accident • Exact location on the site • Sequence of events leading to the accident • Potential cause or causes • Names of witnesses These records may be used as evidence in subsequent investigations, compensation claims, and legal proceedings. Step 3: Report the Injury to the Supervisor The injured worker, or a colleague acting on their behalf, must report the accident to the site supervisor or management as soon as possible. In making this report, record: • The name and position of the person who received the report • The date and time the report was submitted These details will be added to the accident record and may be required for insurance, regulatory reporting, or legal purposes. Step 4: Preserve Evidence Evidence from the accident scene must be preserved promptly. This includes: • Photographing the victim's injuries (with consent) • Photographing the location where the accident occurred • Photographing the equipment, tools, or materials involved • Securing the scene to prevent interference or further incidents

Summary and Revision Questions Lecture Summary — Key Points • Safety is the condition of hazard-free production; it is the inverse of accident rate. • Risk combines probability of loss with magnitude of potential harm. • Hazards are unsafe conditions or acts; accidents are their unforeseen consequences. • Falls from height account for 56% of construction fatalities in Tanzania. • The main causes of accidents are human factors, faulty work methods, and structural failures. • Scaffolding hazards include falls, electrocution, falling objects, and collapse. • PPE is a last line of defence — it does not eliminate hazards at source. • Warning signs use a standardised colour-coding system (notice, caution, warning, danger). • A Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) proactively identifies hazards before work begins. • After an accident: obtain medical care, record details, report to supervisor, preserve evidence. Home Work 1. Distinguish between the terms 'risk', 'hazard', 'safety', and 'accident' with appropriate examples from construction practice. 2. With reference to Tanzanian statistics, analyse the major causes of fatalities on construction sites. What preventive measures would you recommend? 3. Describe four hazards associated with improper scaffolding procedures. For each, state the preventive measure. 4. A contractor is about to commence excavation works for a building foundation. Prepare a Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) worksheet for this activity. 5. Explain the hierarchy of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) categories. Why is PPE considered a 'last resort' rather than a primary safety measure? 6. As a site manager, a worker in your team has just been injured in a fall from a ladder. Describe the four steps you would follow in the immediate aftermath. 7. Using the warning sign colour -coding system, design an appropriate signage plan for a multi -storey building construction site in Tanzania. END OF LECTURE 7 NOTES
